title: The Book of Enoch: A Black Reader's Study Edition
subtitle: The complete text of 1 Enoch, kept whole by an African church, read closely for the people it was carried to
description:
One hundred and eight chapters. One ancient cry from the underside of empire. And one African church that kept the whole book alive.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church calls it Maṣḥafa Henok. Most Christians have never read it. The Book of Enoch: A Black Reader’s Study Edition prints all of 1 Enoch in R. H. Charles’s classic 1917 translation — made from the Ethiopic — and walks you through it, section by section, with a clear and carefully sourced commentary.

It is two books woven together: the Reading Text itself, by chapter and verse, and a study written for Black readers of the Bible in the United States and for anyone who wants to read alongside them. The study follows Enoch through the Watchers, the Parables and the Son of Man, the Astronomical Book and its calendar, the Dream Visions with their history told in animals, and the Epistle of Enoch with its woes and its hope — and then asks what the book leaves in our hands.

Every reading is marked as a reading. The text says. The scholars or the Church say. I read this as. You can always check the page.

What’s inside

  • The complete text of 1 Enoch (chapters 1–108) in R. H. Charles’s 1917 translation, with his own brackets and section headings kept.
  • 31 chapters of commentary in seven parts — from “Which Enoch?” to “What Enoch Leaves Us.”
  • The Reader’s Charter and “Five Things to Carry” — practical convictions to take out of the room, each with a question for a reading circle.
  • An Atlas of the Book and A Timeline — to keep the whole structure in view.
  • Where the English Leaves the Ge’ez — an honest appendix on the limits of the reading text.
  • The Foundation Ledger, a Source Guide, Glossary, Bibliography and Index — every index entry is a link.

An honest edition

The reading text is Charles’s public-domain translation, not a new one, and it has not yet been checked line by line against a Ge’ez manuscript; the book says so plainly. It also takes up hard questions directly, including a chapter on how the color words in Enoch’s animal vision have been used against Black readers. This is an independent work of study, not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and it does not speak for it.

Digital edition (PDF), 527 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase. A free Study Circle Guide for groups is available on the Free Resources page.

who_for:
• Bible readers who have heard of Enoch and want to read the whole book, not just quotations from it.
  • Black Christians and readers of African heritage who want to read the book an African church kept, in conversation with their own tradition.
  • Pastors, teachers and small-group leaders (with a free seven-session study guide).
  • Curious readers who want a sourced, calm alternative to sensational claims about “the forbidden book.”
  • Students who want chapter-and-verse references, an apparatus and an honest account of the text.

No background in Ge’ez, Hebrew or Greek is needed. No one is asked to change churches or canons.

faq.question: What format is the book, and how do I get it?
faq.answer: It is a digital PDF edition of 527 pages. After you check out, sign in to your Account page with the email you used to buy and press Download; you can download it again any time.

faq.question: Does it contain the full text of the Book of Enoch?
faq.answer: Yes. All one hundred and eight chapters of 1 Enoch are printed in full, in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation made from the Ethiopic, together with the commentary.

faq.question: Is this a new translation?
faq.answer: No. The reading text is Charles's public-domain translation. The book states clearly that it is not a new translation and has not yet been checked line by line against a Ge'ez manuscript, and an appendix shows where the English leaves the Ge'ez.

faq.question: Is this an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church?
faq.answer: No. It is an independent work of study. It listens to the church that kept the book, but it does not speak for it or for any other church body.

faq.question: Do I need to read The Ethiopian Canon first?
faq.answer: No. This volume stands on its own. The two books belong to the same series, and The Ethiopian Canon explains how the Ethiopian church counts its books, but you can begin with Enoch.

faq.question: Is there a study guide for groups?
faq.answer: Yes. A free Study Circle Guide turns the book into seven sessions (or fourteen weeks) for Bible studies, classes, book clubs and families. Download it from the Free Resources page.

faq.question: Can I share my copy or print it?
faq.answer: The commentary, notes and tables are protected by copyright and may not be copied or distributed without permission, apart from brief quotations. The free Study Circle Guide may be shared freely for non-commercial study.
